question.prompt: A circle with integer radius \(r\) is centered at \((r,r).\) Distinct line segments of length \(c_i\) connect points \((0,a_i)\) to \((b_i,0)\) for \(1\le i\le14\) and are tangent to the circle, where \(a_i,\) \(b_i,\) and \(c_i\) are all positive integers and \(c_1\le c_2\le\cdots\le c_{14}.\) What is the ratio \(\dfrac{c_{14}}{c_1}\) for the least possible value of \(r?\)

solutions.title: Turn tangency into a factor equation
solutions.explanation:
The line containing a segment is tangent exactly when its distance from \((r,r)\) equals \(r\). This converts the geometry into an equation whose integer solutions can be counted.

Consider one segment, with endpoints \(A=(0,a)\) and \(B=(b,0)\) and length \(c\). Its line has equation
\[
\frac{x}{b}+\frac{y}{a}=1,
\quad\text{or}\quad
ax+by-ab=0.
\]
By the Pythagorean theorem, \(c^2=a^2+b^2\). The point-to-line distance formula therefore gives
\[
\frac{|r(a+b)-ab|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}=r.
\]
Squaring and simplifying yields
\[
ab\bigl(ab-2r(a+b)+2r^2\bigr)=0.
\]
Since \(a,b>0\), this is equivalent to
\[
(a-2r)(b-2r)=2r^2. \tag{1}
\]

We also need the converse, so that counting solutions of (1) counts actual segments. If positive integers \(a,b\) satisfy (1), then
\[
a^2+b^2=(a+b-2r)^2.
\]
Thus the segment has positive integer length \(c=|a+b-2r|\). Substitution into the distance formula gives distance \(r\), so its line is tangent. The circle lies entirely in the closed first quadrant, and the part of the line in that quadrant is exactly \(AB\). Hence the contact point lies on the segment.

Set \(x=a-2r\) and \(y=b-2r\). Equation (1) becomes \(xy=2r^2\), so \(x,y\) have the same sign. Each positive divisor \(x\) determines exactly one positive ordered pair \((x,y)\), and every such pair gives positive \(a,b\). Negative pairs can contribute at most the same number of additional segments.

Let \(d(M)\) denote the number of positive divisors of \(M\). If \(M\) has prime factorization \(\prod p^e\), then \(d(M)=\prod(e+1)\), because a divisor independently chooses each prime exponent from \(0\) through \(e\). We obtain:

| \(r\) | \(2r^2\) | \(d(2r^2)\) | Upper bound on all segments |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| \(1\) | \(2\) | 2 | 4 |
| \(2\) | \(2^3\) | 4 | 8 |
| \(3\) | \(2\cdot3^2\) | 6 | 12 |
| \(4\) | \(2^5\) | 6 | 12 |
| \(5\) | \(2\cdot5^2\) | 6 | 12 |

Thus \(r\ge6\).

At \(r=6\), the product is \(72=2^3\cdot3^2\), giving \(12\) positive ordered factor pairs. For a negative pair, write \(x=-u\), \(y=-v\). Positivity of \(a=12-u\) and \(b=12-v\) requires
\[
u,v<12,\qquad uv=72.
\]
Among the unordered positive factor pairs
\[
(1,72),(2,36),(3,24),(4,18),(6,12),(8,9),
\]
only \((8,9)\) has both entries below \(12\). Its two orders produce \((a,b)=(4,3)\) and \((3,4)\), both of length \(5\). There are therefore exactly \(12+2=14\) segments at the least radius \(r=6\).

For the positive pairs, the length is
\[
c=x+y+12.
\]
It exceeds \(5\). Also,
\[
(x-1)(y-1)\ge0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x+y\le xy+1=73.
\]
Equality occurs for \((x,y)=(1,72)\), giving the largest length \(85\). Thus
\[
\frac{c_{14}}{c_1}=\frac{85}{5}=\boxed{17},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

solutions.title: Use equal tangent lengths
solutions.explanation:
The circle is already tangent to both axes, so equal tangent lengths relate its radius directly to the three sides of a right triangle.

Let \(O=(0,0)\), \(A=(0,a)\), and \(B=(b,0)\). Let \(T\) be the point where \(AB\) touches the circle. The axis contact points are \(U=(0,r)\) and \(V=(r,0)\). The two tangent segments from any external point have equal lengths, so
\[
AT=AU=|a-r|,
\qquad
BT=BV=|b-r|.
\]
Because \(T\) lies on \(AB\),
\[
c=|a-r|+|b-r|.
\]
If \(r\) lay between \(a\) and \(b\), this would give \(c=|a-b|\), contradicting \(c^2=a^2+b^2\) for positive \(a,b\). Thus there are two possibilities:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
a,b>r:&c=a+b-2r,\\
a,b<r:&c=2r-a-b.
\end{array}
\]
Equivalently, the radius is either
\[
r=\frac{a+b-c}{2}
\quad\text{or}\quad
r=\frac{a+b+c}{2}. \tag{1}
\]
These are the radii of the right triangle's incircle and its excircle opposite \(O\). The latter is the circle across \(AB\) from \(O\), tangent to \(AB\) and the extensions of the two legs. Their centers are obtained from the appropriate angle bisectors: a point on an angle bisector is equidistant from its two side lines. Both centers lie on \(y=x\), so a circle of radius \(r\) has center \((r,r)\). Thus both possibilities in (1) are realized.

Squaring \(c=|a+b-2r|\) and using the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
(a-2r)(b-2r)=2r^2. \tag{2}
\]
Conversely, positive integers satisfying (2) have integer hypotenuse \(|a+b-2r|\), and (1) realizes the required circle. We can therefore count signed factor pairs in (2).

For \(r=1,2,3,4,5\), the numbers \(2r^2\) are
\[
2,8,18,32,50,
\]
with respectively \(2,4,6,6,6\) positive divisors. These counts follow by choosing prime exponents in a divisor. Each divisor determines one ordered positive factor pair, and at most one ordered negative pair with the same absolute values. Consequently, these radii allow at most \(4,8,12,12,12\) segments, all fewer than \(14\).

At \(r=6\), the positive shifts \(a-12,b-12\) have product \(72\). There are \((3+1)(2+1)=12\) positive ordered pairs. Negative shifts require their absolute values to be below \(12\); only \(8\) and \(9\) work, in either order. The complete list of triangles, shown with \(a<b\), is:

| \(a\) | \(b\) | \(c=|a+b-12|\) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 | 4 | 5 |
| 20 | 21 | 29 |
| 18 | 24 | 30 |
| 16 | 30 | 34 |
| 15 | 36 | 39 |
| 14 | 48 | 50 |
| 13 | 84 | 85 |

The last six rows arise from the positive factor pairs \((8,9),(6,12),(4,18),(3,24),(2,36),(1,72)\); the first comes from shifts \((-9,-8)\). Swapping \(a,b\) gives a second distinct segment in every row. Thus these are exactly the \(14\) segments at the least radius.

The smallest and largest lengths are \(5\) and \(85\), so
\[
\frac{c_{14}}{c_1}=\frac{85}{5}=\boxed{17},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
